extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency policymakers, judges, and practitioners interested in agency rulemaking/adjudication and Chevron deference
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and practical guidance on when and how federal agencies may develop policy through adjudicative orders rather than notice-and-comment rulemaking, and how courts should treat such policies (including Chevron deference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of policymaking by adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent a specific statutory provision to the contrary, the APA and Supreme Court precedents permit federal agencies to articulate new policy through both rules and adjudicative orders (Chenery II and subsequent cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies have a "very definite place for the case-by-case evolution of statutory standards" and the choice between proceeding by general rule or individual adjudication "lies primarily in the informed discretion of the administrative agency." Courts have repeatedly upheld agencies' discretion to select method unless prohibited by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discretion in method choice must be fact-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of whether to use rulemaking or adjudication is a fact-specific decision that lies primarily within agencies' informed discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and precedents indicate agencies should weigh the plusses and minuses of both methods; courts will overturn an agency choice only if it is "unwarranted in law or . . . without justification in fact."

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudicatory policymaking may be retrospective; retroactivity is not fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudications can have retroactive effect and "such action . . . having a retroactive effect [is] not necessarily fatal to its validity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts balance retroactivity concerns against "the mischief of producing a result which is contrary to a statutory design or to legal and equitable principles." New interpretations in cases of first impression inevitably have retroactive implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tethering to existing law / fair notice requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies cannot create policy by adjudication without there being some existing law to which agencies tether an interpretation, providing the fair notice required by the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory provisions must give "fair warning" of prohibited conduct; agencies must anchor interpretations to statutes or regulations so parties have notice of the legal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and fair-warning standard (person of ordinary intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A policy’s notice must be sufficient that "regulated parties should know what is required of them" and be declared with such "precision" that courts can ensure enforcement is not arbitrary or discriminatory; agencies must "provide a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower courts ask whether a regulation/policy gives "the person of ordinary intelligence a reasonable opportunity to know what is prohibited" and whether it is "reasonably comprehensible to people of good faith."

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against penalizing good-faith reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies cannot penalize persons for past actions taken in good-faith reliance on prior agency pronouncements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although new interpretations can emerge, courts have long prohibited penalizing reliance on prior settled course of action; agencies should avoid substituting new law for old law that was "reasonably clear."

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on changing clearly established law without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may not "substitut[e] . . . new law for old law that was reasonably clear" in adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an established rule has been generally recognized and relied upon, altering it in an adjudication can raise retroactivity and unfair-surprise concerns; courts may refuse retroactive application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to base adjudicatory policy on adjudicative facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies developed through adjudications must be based upon "adjudicative facts specifically relevant to the circumstances" of the litigant rather than solely legislative facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency constructs a rule of general applicability in an adjudication without examining specific facts tied to the litigant, courts may find an abuse of discretion (First Bancorporation and similar cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using adjudication as a vehicle for general rules without facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies cannot use a single adjudication as the vehicle for a rule of general applicability absent consideration of the case's specific facts and particularized relevance to the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have overturned agency orders that function as generalized rules where no specific adjudicative facts were examined and the rule lacked particularized relevance to the litigant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards to ensure litigant procedural protections (due process parity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must afford litigants in adjudications the same rule-of-law protections as provided in Article III cases, ensuring due process is not violated when agencies articulate new policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections operate alongside APA reasoned-decisionmaking requirements; agencies should ensure adequate notice, opportunity to be heard, and reasoned explanation tied to facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unfair surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must avoid creating 'unfair surprise' by applying new policies retroactively in ways that would be fundamentally unfair or unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have articulated a 'fair warning' and 'unfair surprise' doctrine: if application would unfairly surprise regulated parties, the agency's adjudicatory change should not be applied retroactively — it should apply prospectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settled-course constraint on abrupt departures
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s abrupt departure from a 'general policy by which its exercise of discretion will be governed' — including a 'settled course of adjudication' — can be arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settled course requires a clear and consistent line of prior adjudications; "one favorable exercise of discretion does not a settled course make." Courts review a series of decisions to determine whether a settled practice existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When adjudication is especially appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication is 'especially appropriate' when 'it is doubtful whether any generalized standard could be framed which would have more than marginal utility' and the agency needs to "develop[] its standards in a case-by-case manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudication is suitable for highly specialized, varying, or unforeseeable problems that resist generic regulatory formulation (NLRB v. Bell Aerospace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies can use adjudication to resolve classes of issues not requiring case-by-case consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a statutory scheme contemplates individualized determinations, the decisionmaker may rely on rulemaking to resolve certain issues of general applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may issue regulations in adjudications to resolve classes of issues unless Congress clearly withheld that authority (American Hospital Association). This avoids needless relitigation of certain issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication's comparative benefits as a policymaking method
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication can offer benefits over informal rulemaking: speed, case-by-case policy development, ex post policy clarification, increased policymaking opportunities, opportunity to observe regulated actions, and ability to reverse course quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consider adjudication where these benefits outweigh the prospective rulemaking advantages; adjudication can produce tailored policies and increase participation by marginalized communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking's burdens that favor adjudication in some cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal rulemaking has acquired many layers of judicial, executive, and legislative procedural requirements that slow and complicate rulemaking (e.g., exhaustive preamble responses, cost–benefit analyses, White House review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where rulemaking is likely to be ossified or delayed by such requirements, agencies should consider adjudication as a more efficient alternative while maintaining accountability safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-participation practices to make adjudication as legitimate as rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication can provide as much rational reason-giving and accountability as informal rulemaking if agencies broadly permit public participation (e.g., intervention, amicus briefing, oral argument, publishing notice in the Federal Register of opportunities for public input, informing the public of newly articulated policies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementing these participation practices can bolster the legitimacy of adjudicatory policymaking and support claims for deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docketing and publication to improve discoverability
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt public docketing systems, publish precedential decisions (with summaries), and offer subscription/notification services so the public can learn about and comment on policy-changing adjudications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include BIA's publication of precedential decisions and summaries; agencies can also issue press releases, guidance, and compile adjudicatory holdings akin to the CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give notice of potential policy-changing adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency believes it may decide a case in a way that is precedent-setting or policy-changing, it could place a notice in the Federal Register that describes the issues in the case (or link to the case’s docket or filings) and solicits amicus briefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies could receive briefs through regulations.gov, as many do for rulemakings, enabling public comment on adjudications much as on rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to material comments and amicus briefs in the adjudication's opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure accountability akin to rulemaking, agencies should respond on the record to amici comments and material arguments raised in adjudications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies already respond to comments in rulemaking preambles; courts can examine whether agencies addressed material arguments offered in amicus briefs when assessing adequacy of reason-giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and label precedential adjudications and publicize new policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should identify cases as precedential, publish them on websites, issue press releases or guidance describing new holdings, and compile holdings into accessible compendiums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such practices make it easier for regulated parties and courts to find and understand new adjudicatory policies, reducing unfair-surprise concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for Chevron deference to adjudicatory policymaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudicatory policies warrant Chevron deference because Congress delegated policymaking authority to agencies, and deference is appropriate where agencies articulate rationales and permit non-agency parties an opportunity to provide information agencies may not have considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference should be available when agencies demonstrate delegation/expertise, provide reasoned explanation, and open a path for public participation (intervention, amicus briefs, notice). Courts should not exclude adjudications from Chevron deference solely based on form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative solutions to concerns about Chevron administrability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than categorically limiting deference to formal adjudications, agencies can obtain deference by meeting four practical requirements: advertise a policymaking, provide a comment opportunity, respond to material comments, and publish/publicize the new policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deference is conditioned on these four steps, agencies will adopt them; administrability concerns can be solved operationally rather than by a bright-line formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective application when unfair surprise found
rubrics_metrics.description: When an adjudicatory policy change would create unfair surprise, courts should apply the new policy prospectively only (i.e., not to penalize parties who relied on prior understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves rule-of-law protections while allowing the policy to guide future conduct; courts already apply prospectivity remedies in such situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should leave gaps for adjudication in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Where agencies must use rulemaking, they should consider leaving more gaps for adjudication so the law can develop gradually and as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic delegation within regulations can speed implementation and permit case-by-case refinement via adjudication rather than trying to legislate every detail in a single rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review standard for agency method choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will defer to an agency's selection of adjudication vs rulemaking unless the choice is 'unwarranted in law or . . . without justification in fact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review focuses on whether the agency examined the relevant facts and provided a reasoned basis for its choice of method (Butz, Chenery II and successors).
